name: Nishiki Market Alley by MOON and BACK

claims.text: This is a ramen shop with a mixed kitchen, not a dedicated gluten-free facility, so cross-contact is possible and severe celiacs should confirm protocols directly. That said, reviewers report the gluten-free noodles are boiled in a separate boiler from the regular wheat noodles.
At the Nishiki Market Alley location, reviewers report staff confirmed they use a separate fryer to help prevent cross-contamination.

Standard soy sauce in Japanese ramen typically contains wheat. MOON and BACK offers gluten-free soy sauce on request, so ask for the gluten-free version with your order rather than assuming the default broth or sushi sauce is wheat-free.

The kitchen is mixed, serving meat alongside vegan dishes. One vegan reviewer noted that most other diners order the raw Wagyu beef ramen that is blowtorched tableside, which fills the small space with 'meat air' - worth knowing if that bothers you, though it does not affect the vegan ingredients themselves.
The vegan ramen is described as made entirely from naturally fermented miso and soy milk with no animal ingredients, and the menu labels vegan items clearly.
Multiple reviewers report staff immediately ask about allergies and dietary restrictions when you sit down, and that most staff speak good English, making it easier to discuss your needs.

Coeliac reviewers report that staff know what celiac disease means and ask about allergies when you order, and several said they felt very safe eating there - but always confirm your own protocols, as it is not a dedicated gluten-free kitchen.
The menu is clearly labeled for what is vegan and what is gluten-free, and dedicated vegan and gluten-free ramen are standing menu items rather than improvised substitutions.

Gluten-free noodles are rice-based, gluten-free soy sauce is available on request, and reviewers report a separate noodle boiler and a separate fryer at the Nishiki location - meaningful precautions for a non-dedicated kitchen.
English-speaking staff and a stated whole-restaurant philosophy of safe food for guests with allergies and dietary restrictions make it an unusually accommodating ramen stop near Nishiki Market.

Not celiac-safe based on documented cooking. The menu features vegetable tempura and fritters, which in Japanese kitchens are battered with wheat flour, creating a strong risk of gluten in fried items and shared frying oil. No information confirms a dedicated gluten-free fryer or separate prep, so cross-contamination should be assumed.

Sauces and dressings appear throughout the menu (for example dishes finished with soy-based sauces and a curry soy-milk mayo). Standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so seasonings here likely contain gluten unless the restaurant confirms a wheat-free tamari. Celiac diners should verify each sauce directly.

Strongly vegan-friendly by design: the kitchen uses only vegetables and explicitly avoids animal-derived ingredients, eggs, and dairy across the whole menu, so the baseline risk of animal-product cross-contact is low. No information is documented on shared oil or surfaces, so strict vegans who avoid trace contact should still confirm.
An entirely plant-based kitchen that avoids animal products, eggs, and dairy, which makes it a comfortable choice for vegan diners.
Whole-food, vegetable-forward cooking with brown rice and many small seasonal plates, so diners can see and ask about each component.

MOS Burger's low-allergen burger and hot dog arrive in individually sealed packaging, and the chain states there is no chance for allergens to get into the package at the store, which lowers cross-contamination risk for these specific items. However, the kitchen is not a dedicated gluten-free facility, so the regular menu shares wheat-handling equipment.

Most standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Coverage of MOS Burger's allergen program notes that allergens can hide even in soy sauce, so any item with regular sauces should be assumed to contain wheat unless the sealed low-allergen item is chosen.

No vegan-specific cross-contact information was documented. The low-allergen burger and hot dog are pork-based, and vegan status is not addressed in the sources, so ingredients should be confirmed with staff.
The low-allergen menu is designed to exclude egg, milk, wheat, shrimp, crab, soba (buckwheat) and peanut, and items are prepared and sealed so allergens cannot enter the package at the store.

The low-allergen burger and hot dog use rice-flour buns instead of wheat and come in pre-sealed packs, making them a relatively safe option for wheat avoiders; the buns are described as soft and surprisingly filling.
These low-allergen items are part of the kids' menu but can be purchased by adults as well.

The cafe offers some gluten-free menu items (including a Sesame Miso Soy Milk Ramen Set and several desserts marked gluten-free), but states plainly that the kitchen is NOT a dedicated gluten-free kitchen and that utensils and dishes may carry traces of wheat. This means it cannot be considered safe for celiac diners — treat the GF items as lower-gluten, not zero-risk, and confirm directly if you are highly sensitive.

Several dishes use a soy-sauce base (e.g. the fried okara-konjac in the signature set). Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) typically contains wheat, so soy-sauce-seasoned items should be assumed to contain wheat unless staff confirm a wheat-free tamari is used. The existing note that tamari may be available on request points to this being a per-dish, ask-the-staff situation.

Cross-contact risk for vegans is structurally low: the entire kitchen is animal-product-free — no eggs, dairy, meat, or fish are used anywhere — so there are no animal ingredients in the kitchen to cross-contaminate with.
Even the dashi/stock is plant-based (kombu and shiitake), removing the most common hidden-animal pitfall (fish/bonito stock) found in Japanese cooking.
The English menu clearly lists information important to vegans, such as whether fish stock is used, which makes it easier to identify what is safe before ordering.

The cafe explicitly welcomes guests with allergies alongside vegans and vegetarians, framing the whole menu around being able to dine 'with peace of mind' — but for specific allergen questions it is best to confirm with staff, as detailed cross-contamination protocols are not published.
100% vegan kitchen — no animal-derived ingredients of any kind, so animal-product cross-contact is not a concern for vegan diners.
Also avoids eggs, dairy, refined sugar, and chemical seasonings, and uses plant-based kombu/shiitake dashi.
Offers a dedicated set of gluten-free menu items and is upfront about the kitchen not being a dedicated GF environment, which lets sensitive diners make an informed choice.

This is a wheat-based ramen shop and is not celiac-safe. The house noodles are made from selected domestic wheat, and the kitchen's two signature broths include a spicy miso broth (miso commonly contains barley or wheat). Even non-noodle items share a kitchen built around wheat noodles, so cross-contamination is very likely. No gluten-free menu or dedicated gluten-free preparation is documented.
The restaurant states allergy information is available on request and staff can help with dietary needs, but no specific gluten-free protocol, separate cookware, or celiac accommodation is described.

The shop uses a spicy miso broth and standard Japanese seasonings; like most Japanese soy sauce and miso, these typically contain wheat. Assume the seasonings are not gluten-free unless staff confirm a wheat-free version.

Dedicated vegan ramen (a plain and a spicy version) is on the menu, so plant-based diners do have real options here — but this is primarily a beef and halal wagyu ramen kitchen, so vegan bowls are cooked alongside meat dishes and wheat noodles. Strict vegans concerned about shared equipment or broth should confirm preparation with staff.

The restaurant offers an English menu with photos and says allergy information is available on request, with staff available to help address dietary needs. No specifics on how allergens are isolated in the kitchen are published.
Pork-free, halal-certified kitchen using only A5-grade halal wagyu, with vegan and vegetarian ramen options and a prayer room — a genuinely inclusive setup for Muslim, vegan, and vegetarian diners.
A vegan diner praised the spicy vegan ramen as filling and full of flavor, with soy bits adding texture (note: feedback on the plain vegan ramen was mixed).

Gluten-free donuts and bread are offered and praised by GF diners, but no source documents whether they are prepared in a dedicated, gluten-free-only area or fryer, so cross-contact cannot be confirmed. Celiac diners should confirm prep directly with staff.

No source specifies whether the soy sauce or seasonings used are gluten-free. As most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, anyone avoiding gluten should ask which sauces are used on the lunch set and vegan karaage.

The kitchen has been fully vegan since September 2025, with no animal products on the menu, so the risk of animal-derived cross-contact is low by design. Plant milks (oat and soy) are available for drinks.
Staff are described as friendly and the food as made with care, and menu items are labelled as vegan/gluten-free, but no specific allergy-handling protocol is documented in the sources.
Reviewers consistently praise the gluten-free tofu donuts and gluten-free set as very good.
Fully vegan kitchen with clearly labelled items and seasonal, house-made cooking; the philosophy is that vegan and gluten-free should not mean compromising on taste.

This branch carries the same chain menu as MOS Burger Japan-wide, including the low-allergen sealed-pack rice-burger and hot dog, which are prepared and sealed off-site to limit allergen contact. No location-specific cross-contamination protocol is documented for the open kitchen, so confirm handling with staff on the day.

MOS publishes an English allergen list (PDF) and notes that ingredients can vary by store and that information is not fully guaranteed, so celiac diners should rely on the sealed low-allergen items rather than the standard menu.

MOS's signature Teriyaki Burger sauce is built on Japanese teriyaki, which is made with soy sauce that typically contains wheat — so the regular burgers, sauces and most of the standard menu are not celiac-safe.

A vegetable burger (MOS Yasai Burger) is on the menu, but it is not certified vegan and is prepared in a shared kitchen alongside meat and dairy items; standard sauces and buns may contain egg, milk or animal-derived ingredients. Vegans should ask staff to check ingredients and preparation.

The chain-wide low-allergen rice-burger and hot dog are certified gluten-free and free of wheat, egg and milk, and arrive in sealed plastic packaging — a rare reliable option for celiac and multi-allergy diners at a burger shop.
MOS provides an allergen list in English and cooks each item fresh to order, which can make it easier to ask about and confirm ingredients.

This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop, so it should be treated as NOT celiac-safe. Even the vegan ramen is explicitly made with whole-wheat (zenryufun) noodles, meaning every bowl on the menu contains wheat. No gluten-free noodle or dedicated gluten-free preparation is documented.

Wheat noodles are sourced from a noodle maker (Kiyokawa Seimen in Chichibu); the same noodle pots and broths serve all bowls, so cross-contamination with gluten is effectively unavoidable for a strict celiac diner.

The salt-based bowls are seasoned with 'white tamari' (shiro-tamari), a naturally brewed seasoning from Iga, Mie. White tamari is typically brewed mostly from wheat, so it should be assumed to contain wheat/gluten unless the shop confirms otherwise.

A dedicated vegan ramen is on the menu (including a 100% vegan Shinshu-miso version and a 'tonkotsu-style' vegetable bowl), and the shop reportedly gets frequent vegan inquiries from international visitors. However, the broths for the regular menu are made from chicken bones, pork and bonito/dashi, and there is no documented separation of cookware or noodle water, so vegan diners should confirm how the vegan bowl is cooked relative to the meat and fish broths.
A genuine, clearly labeled vegan ramen is part of the standard menu, and the shop is used to fielding vegan questions from overseas guests — a good sign for being able to discuss dietary needs.
